ed.name: Tunisia
ed.stripDate: Expected between November 2027 and March 2028 (date not set)
facts: Legislative vote (Assembly of the Representatives of the People, 161 seats)
Not set · an ISIE council member points to November 2027
Last 3 months of the 5-year term (the Assembly first sat on 13 March 2023)
4 · candidates run as individuals, not on party lists
system: Presidential republic under the 2022 constitution, which President Kaïs Saïed wrote after shutting down the elected parliament by decree in July 2021. The President is elected for five years and may serve at most two full terms. Parliament has two chambers: the Assembly of the Representatives of the People (ARP), elected directly for five years, and the National Council of Regions and Districts, whose members are chosen by and from regional councils. The new Assembly has far less power than the parliament it replaced.

Decree-law 55 of September 2022 replaced party-list voting with two-round contests between individual candidates for the Assembly’s 161 seats. Each candidate needs 400 voter sponsorships, there is no public campaign funding, and voters can withdraw confidence from their deputy. Ballots carry no party labels, so most deputies elected in 2022–23 sit as independents. Vacant seats are filled by by-elections, such as the one held in El Kabaria (Tunis) in 2026.

The constitution requires the ARP election in the last three months of the five-year term, and the current Assembly first sat on 13 March 2023. The electoral authority (ISIE), chaired by Farouk Bouasker, is budgeting for legislative and municipal elections in 2027. ISIE council member Belgacem Ayachi said on 13 October 2026 that the legislative vote would take place in November 2027, stressing that this is not an officially adopted calendar. He said municipal elections could come before the end of 2026, or otherwise by March 2027, once a decree convening voters is published.
Not a competitive vote in the usual sense

Most opposition parties boycotted the 2022–23 legislative vote: the National Salvation Front, which includes Ennahdha, announced its boycott in early September 2022, and a coalition of five parties including the Workers’ Party and Al Joumhouri followed. Turnout was about 11%, and the Front refused to recognise the new parliament. Since then opposition leaders have received heavy sentences: Ennahdha leader Rached Ghannouchi was given a life sentence in June 2026, and PDL leader Abir Moussi’s prison sentences were upheld in September 2026. Ennahdha says opponents, activists, journalists and businesspeople are jailed on unfounded charges; the authorities deny holding anyone for political reasons.

From 1973 wages were set in talks between the government, the UGTT union and the employers’ union UTICA. The 2026 finance law lets the government set wage rises for 2026–2028 itself. The UGTT called a general strike for 21 January 2026 to demand negotiations and protest the crackdown on critics; this edition could not confirm whether it went ahead. After a period of internal tensions, the union’s congress in Monastir (25–27 March 2026) elected Salaheddine Selmi as secretary general; he says the union’s hand is “held out to dialogue” with the government.

Because ballots carry no party labels, this edition compares four political forces, not lists: President Saïed’s camp, coded from his and his government’s record (he has no party); Echaab, which backed the 25 July 2021 measures and now calls itself an opposition party; Ennahdha, coded from its statements while its leaders are in prison; and the UGTT, a union that fields no candidates but is central on wages and public spending. In 2027 you will vote for an individual candidate, who may or may not be close to one of them.
ed.status: This is not a competitive election in the usual sense. Candidates run as individuals with no party labels. Most opposition parties boycotted the last legislative vote in 2022–23, among them Ennahdha and its allies in the National Salvation Front, the Workers’ Party and Al Joumhouri. Several opposition leaders are in prison, including Ennahdha’s Rached Ghannouchi and the PDL’s Abir Moussi. In the sources found, no party had said whether it will take part in 2027. Positions were therefore coded from records and statements published up to 18 October 2026. President Saïed has no party, so his column codes his own and his government’s record (laws, decrees, budgets). Echaab, Ennahdha and the UGTT are coded from their published statements. The UGTT is a trade union, not a party, and fields no candidates. The PDL is not compared because no recent policy statement was found. Several positions date from 2021–2022 and are marked as older. Research for this edition was cut short: almost half the questions code only one force, and Ennahdha and the UGTT are each coded on about a third of them. Nothing here has been validated by the parties, the UGTT or an independent committee.

questions.text: Tunisia should agree a loan programme with the IMF, even if it comes with reform conditions.
questions.ctx: Talks on a new IMF programme have been stalled since 2023. The 2026 budget relies instead on domestic borrowing, including an exceptional loan from the Central Bank. Supporters of an IMF deal say it would unlock cheaper foreign lending and reassure markets; opponents say its conditions, such as spending cuts and wage restraint, would hurt purchasing power and limit the country’s sovereignty.

tn_25j.n: The government built its 2026 budget on Central Bank borrowing and a wealth tax “after spurning a potential IMF bailout” (Bloomberg, October 2025).

tn_ugtt.n: In June 2022, while the government sought an IMF loan tied to unpopular reforms such as wage freezes, the UGTT called a strike in 159 state companies, rejecting proposed spending cuts and demanding wage rises.

nd.tn_echaab: Echaab warned in 2022 against a “liberal approach” that puts economic concerns before social ones, but this edition found no Echaab statement on an IMF programme.
nd.tn_nahdha: Ennahdha describes an acute economic and social crisis (January 2026) but proposed no economic measures in the statement found.

questions.short: Central Bank lends to the state
questions.text: The Central Bank should keep lending directly to the state to cover the budget.
questions.ctx: The 2026 budget plans an exceptional loan of about $3.7 billion from the Central Bank of Tunisia, after about $2.3 billion in 2025; what began as a temporary post-pandemic measure has become a regular feature of the budget. The government says this is needed to preserve the continuity of public services. Economists warn of inflation, a weaker dinar, less liquidity for banks and less credit for private firms.

tn_25j.n: The 2026 draft finance law asks the Central Bank for an exceptional loan of about $3.7 billion, after about $2.3 billion in 2025.

nd.tn_echaab: Echaab criticises incoherent, case-by-case economic management (April 2026), but this edition found no Echaab statement on Central Bank lending.

questions.text: People whose assets exceed 5 million dinars should pay an annual 1% wealth tax.
questions.ctx: The 2026 budget introduces a 1% “solidarity” tax on assets above 5 million dinars, alongside a first sovereign sukuk (Islamic bond) of 7 billion dinars. The deficit is about 6.3% of GDP. Supporters say the wealthiest should contribute more; critics say such taxes are hard to collect and can push capital abroad.

tn_25j.n: The 2026 draft finance law created a 1% solidarity tax on assets above 5 million dinars.

nd.tn_echaab: Echaab says key sectors remain in the hands of a few actors (January 2026), but it did not comment on this tax in the sources found.

questions.text: Breaking the hold of a few companies over key sectors should be a top priority of the next parliament.
questions.ctx: Supporters of the 25 July 2021 measures presented them as a break with corruption and promised to fight monopolies and rent. In January 2026 Echaab leader Zouhair Maghzaoui said key sectors are still controlled by a few actors. Others argue that the priority is to attract investment and that heavy-handed action against large firms can scare it away.

tn_echaab.n: Maghzaoui (January 2026): the 25 July process has not kept its promises against monopolies and rent, and “no major structural reform has been undertaken”.

nd.tn_25j: This edition found no recent law or government statement on breaking up monopolies in the sources opened.

questions.text: Public spending should keep rising to pay for wage increases, even if the budget deficit stays above 6% of GDP.
questions.ctx: The 2026 budget raises spending from 59.8 to 63.5 billion dinars, mainly because of wage increases in the public and private sectors, with a deficit of about 6.3% of GDP and public debt near 81% of GDP. Supporters say this protects purchasing power after years of inflation (7.4% on average in 2024); economists warn of more inflation and of less credit for private firms.

tn_25j.n: The 2026 draft finance law raises spending to 63.5 billion dinars, driven largely by planned wage increases, with a deficit of 6.3% of GDP.

tn_ugtt.n: In June 2022 the UGTT demanded wage increases for state workers and rejected proposed spending cuts; it did not comment on the deficit target in the sources found.

questions.text: The government should set wage increases itself, through the finance law, rather than negotiate them with the UGTT and employers.
questions.ctx: From 1973 wages were set in tripartite talks between the government, the UGTT union and the employers’ union UTICA. The 2026 finance law lets the government set public-sector, private-sector and pension increases for 2026, 2027 and 2028. The Social Affairs minister says the Labour Code allows rises by law or decree and that legal procedures were followed; union structures say this destroys social dialogue and that private-sector wages can only be raised through collective bargaining.

tn_25j.n: Under the 2026 finance law, wage rises for 2026–2028 are set by the government, bypassing tripartite talks; Labour minister Issam Lahmar said they are spread over three years.

tn_ugtt.n: The UGTT called a nationwide general strike for 21 January 2026 to demand wage negotiations; its new leadership wants social dialogue put “back on its normal track”.

nd.tn_echaab: Echaab said in 2021 it would coordinate its positions with the UGTT, but this edition found no Echaab statement on the 2026 wage decision.

questions.text: The state should directly recruit graduates who have been unemployed for many years into the public sector.
questions.ctx: Law 38 provides for the hiring of long-term unemployed graduates. Supporters see it as fair to a generation shut out of work; critics say the public wage bill, budgeted at 25.3 billion dinars for 2026, cannot absorb many more jobs and that private-sector growth is needed instead.

tn_echaab.n: Echaab (April 2022) called for activating Law 38 on hiring long-unemployed graduates, saying young people are a key asset.

nd.tn_25j: This edition could not re-check a recent source on how many graduates the state has hired under Law 38.

questions.text: Parties should again be able to present lists of candidates in legislative elections, instead of individual candidacies only.
questions.ctx: Decree-law 55 of September 2022 replaced list voting with two-round contests between individual candidates, sharply reducing the role of parties, and ballots in 2022–23 carried no party labels. Supporters say this brings deputies closer to local voters; the watchdog Al-Bawsala said it would produce an unrepresentative parliament that favours money and tribal networks.

tn_25j.n: Saïed’s Decree-law 55 (September 2022) introduced individual candidacies in two-round, single-member contests.

nd.tn_nahdha: Ennahdha’s coalition announced its 2022 boycott before this law was published; this edition found no recent Ennahdha proposal on the voting system.
nd.tn_echaab: This edition found no Echaab position on the voting system.

questions.text: Candidates should again receive public funding for their election campaigns.
questions.ctx: Decree-law 55 abolished public campaign funding, so candidates must pay for themselves or use private money. Supporters say this saves public money; Al-Bawsala said it tilts the vote towards candidates with money and clan networks.

tn_25j.n: Decree-law 55 (September 2022) ended public campaign funding, leaving only self-financing and private funding.

questions.text: Candidates for Parliament should no longer need to collect 400 voter sponsorships to stand.
questions.ctx: Decree-law 55 requires each candidate to gather 400 sponsorships from voters. Supporters say it filters out candidacies with no local support; Al-Bawsala called it an “impossible” condition that would make standing a monopoly of moneyed circles or tribal notables.

tn_25j.n: Decree-law 55 (September 2022) set the requirement of 400 voter sponsorships per candidate.

questions.text: Voters should keep the right to withdraw their deputy’s mandate before the end of the term.
questions.ctx: Article 61 of the 2022 constitution allows a deputy’s mandate to be revoked under conditions set by the electoral law, and Decree-law 55 organises this withdrawal of confidence by voters. Supporters say it makes deputies accountable to their constituency; Al-Bawsala called it a tool for blackmailing deputies.

tn_25j.n: The 2022 constitution written by Saïed lets voters revoke a deputy’s mandate (Art. 61), as organised by his Decree-law 55.

questions.text: The elections held since 2022 met the standards of a free and fair vote.
questions.ctx: Turnout in the 2022–23 legislative vote was about 11% after most parties boycotted it, and the parliament elected then has sat since March 2023. Boycotting parties called the vote the last step of a political agenda imposed by the President; Ennahdha says recent elections fell short of free and fair standards. The authorities and the electoral authority stand by the results.

tn_25j.n: The President called the 2022–23 legislative vote under his own electoral law, and the parliament it produced has sat since 13 March 2023.

tn_nahdha.n: Ennahdha (January 2026) says elections have been held “below the standards of free and fair democracy”.

nd.tn_echaab: Echaab took part in the 2024 presidential vote with its own candidate; this edition found no Echaab assessment of whether the elections were free and fair.

questions.text: Opposition parties should take part in the 2027 legislative elections rather than boycott them.
questions.ctx: Most opposition parties boycotted the 2022–23 legislative vote, including the National Salvation Front, which includes Ennahdha, and a five-party coalition including the Workers’ Party and Al Joumhouri; turnout was about 11%. Those in favour of taking part say a boycott leaves the field to the President’s supporters; those in favour of a boycott say the rules and the prosecution of opponents make a fair contest impossible. No party had announced its decision for 2027 in the sources found.

tn_echaab.n: Echaab ran its leader Zouhair Maghzaoui in the 2024 presidential election instead of boycotting it; it had not announced its plans for 2027 in the sources found.

tn_nahdha.n: Ennahdha boycotted the 2022–23 vote within the National Salvation Front and says recent elections fell short of free and fair standards (January 2026); this edition found no decision for 2027.

questions.text: The political path begun on 25 July 2021 – a new constitution, a strong presidency and individual candidacies – should continue.
questions.ctx: In July 2021 President Saïed shut down the elected parliament by decree, then wrote the 2022 constitution and changed the electoral law. Six parties that backed him in 2021 called it a break with a decade of chaos and corruption. Opponents call it a coup or a concentration of power, and some early backers, such as Echaab and the UGTT, later turned critical.

tn_25j.n: Saïed shut the previous parliament in July 2021, wrote the 2022 constitution and governs under it.

tn_echaab.n: Echaab backed the 25 July measures at first but now places itself in opposition; Maghzaoui said in January 2026 that the process has not delivered on its promises.

tn_ugtt.n: The UGTT supported the 2021 shutdown of parliament but later opposed Saïed’s subsequent measures, and in December 2025 protested a crackdown on critics.

tn_nahdha.n: Ennahdha (January 2026) calls the 2021 measures a “coup d’État” and commits to a peaceful, civil and legal struggle to restore the democratic path.

questions.text: The constitution should be changed to give Parliament more power to check the President and the government.
questions.ctx: Under the 2022 constitution the Assembly elected in 2022–23 has far less power than the parliament it replaced. Supporters of the current system say a strong presidency ended years of paralysis; critics say Parliament can no longer hold the executive to account.

tn_25j.n: Saïed wrote the 2022 constitution, under which the new Assembly has far less power than the parliament he shut in 2021.

tn_echaab.n: In December 2021 Echaab said the President “monopolises decision-making power” over the country’s future; in 2024 it noted that real power under the 2022 constitution lies with the President.

tn_nahdha.n: Ennahdha (January 2026) denounces a “deep political deadlock” and repeated attacks on constitutional institutions since 2021; it made no specific proposal on Parliament’s powers.

questions.text: The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Council of the Judiciary should be set up before the 2027 elections.
questions.ctx: The 2022 constitution provides for a nine-member Constitutional Court made up of the most senior judges of the Court of Cassation, the Administrative Court and the Court of Accounts, appointed by order. In April 2026 neither the Court nor a Supreme Council of the Judiciary was in place. Supporters say both are needed to settle disputes and protect rights before the vote; no timetable had been announced in the sources found.

tn_echaab.n: Maghzaoui (April 2026) voiced concern that the Supreme Council of the Judiciary and the Constitutional Court are still missing and urged the President to set them up.

tn_nahdha.n: Ennahdha (January 2026) denounces repeated attacks on constitutional institutions; it did not name these two bodies in the statement found.

nd.tn_25j: The 2022 constitution (Art. 125) provides for the Court, but it had not been set up by April 2026. This edition found no statement by the President on a timetable.

questions.text: Before the 2027 elections, the President should open a national dialogue with parties, the UGTT and civil society, including the opposition.
questions.ctx: In 2022 the President organised an online consultation on reforms, whose shortcomings Echaab criticised. Ennahdha called for an inclusive national dialogue in January 2026, and the UGTT’s new leadership says it cannot remain in a state of rupture with the government. Supporters of a dialogue say it could ease tensions before the vote; others say the 2021–2022 reforms already gave the people their say.

tn_nahdha.n: Ennahdha (January 2026) called for “an inclusive national dialogue”.

tn_echaab.n: In December 2021 Echaab asked the President to “open a dialogue with all national forces” and then hold democratic elections.

tn_ugtt.n: New UGTT secretary general Salaheddine Selmi (March 2026): “the Union’s hand is held out to dialogue”, and “it is not possible to continue in a state of rupture with the government”.

questions.text: Decree-law 54 on information and communication offences should be repealed or deeply amended.
questions.ctx: Echaab’s leader names the revision or repeal of Decree 54 as a priority for freedoms, and the UGTT and Ennahdha denounce the jailing of journalists and critics. Supporters of keeping the decree-law say it is needed against false news and online abuse.

tn_echaab.n: Maghzaoui (January 2026) said freedoms are a central priority, especially the revision or repeal of Decree 54.

tn_ugtt.n: The UGTT’s December 2025 strike call protested eroding freedoms and the crackdown on journalists and critics; it did not single out Decree 54 in the source found.

tn_nahdha.n: Ennahdha (January 2026) says journalists, activists and opponents are jailed on “unfounded accusations”; it did not single out Decree 54 in the statement found.

nd.tn_25j: This edition could not re-check a recent source on the government’s position on amending the decree-law.

questions.text: Opposition leaders and critics jailed since 2023 should be released.
questions.ctx: Since 2023 courts have handed heavy sentences to opposition leaders: Ennahdha leader Rached Ghannouchi received 20 years in one case in April 2026 and life plus 30 years in another in June 2026, and the Court of Cassation upheld PDL leader Abir Moussi’s sentences of 10 and 2 years in September 2026. Ennahdha says many opponents, activists, journalists and businesspeople are jailed after unfair trials; the authorities deny holding anyone for political reasons.

tn_nahdha.n: Ennahdha (January 2026) demands “the release of all political detainees” and an end to unfair trials.

tn_25j.n: Ghannouchi and other leaders received long sentences, and the authorities deny holding anyone for political reasons (June 2026).

tn_echaab.n: Maghzaoui (January 2026) questioned political prosecutions, saying it is “difficult to speak of independent justice”.

tn_ugtt.n: The UGTT’s December 2025 strike call protested the crackdown on opposition leaders, journalists and civil society.

questions.text: Opposition parties and unions should be free to hold marches and strikes against government policy.
questions.ctx: In January 2026 opposition forces held a national march on 10 January, and the UGTT called a general strike for 21 January to demand wage talks and protest a crackdown on critics. Echaab says party activity faces growing restrictions. Others argue that protests and strikes must not paralyse public services or the economy.

tn_nahdha.n: Ennahdha (January 2026) praised the forces that took part in the 10 January national march.

tn_ugtt.n: The UGTT called a nationwide general strike for 21 January 2026, citing eroding freedoms and the crackdown on critics.

tn_echaab.n: Maghzaoui (January 2026) described growing restrictions on party activity.

nd.tn_25j: This edition found no verified government statement on marches or strikes in the sources opened.

questions.text: Tunisian parties and politicians should never seek the support of foreign powers in domestic political disputes.
questions.ctx: Echaab’s leader calls seeking the backing of outside forces a “red line”, and in 2022 the party warned against calls for foreign intervention. Others argue that appealing to international bodies is legitimate when rights are not protected at home.

tn_echaab.n: Maghzaoui (January 2026): reaching out abroad and seeking the support of outside forces “is a red line”.

questions.text: Parliament should pass a law making any normalisation of relations with Israel a crime.
questions.ctx: Echaab calls any normalisation with Israel a betrayal and lists the Palestinian cause among its core goals. Supporters of a law say it would make this stance binding; others say a law is not needed or could harm the country’s external interests.

tn_echaab.n: Echaab (April 2022) called normalisation with Israel a betrayal; this edition found no Echaab statement on a criminalisation law itself.

nd.tn_25j: This edition could not re-check a source on the President’s position on a criminalisation bill.

questions.text: Fuel prices should be raised step by step to reduce the cost of energy subsidies.
questions.ctx: In 2022 the government raised pump prices several times, which Echaab condemned. Supporters of gradual rises say subsidies weigh on the budget and benefit those who consume most; opponents say price rises hit purchasing power already eroded by inflation.

tn_echaab.n: Echaab (April 2022) condemned repeated fuel price rises at a time of falling purchasing power.

tn_25j.n: The government raised fuel prices several times in 2022, as Echaab’s April 2022 statement records; this edition found no verified figures for 2025–2026.

questions.short: Fight high prices case by case
questions.text: To fight high prices, the government should rely mainly on direct interventions on the prices of specific products.
questions.ctx: Echaab’s leader criticises the authorities’ one-off interventions on prices for not tackling the causes of high prices, and calls for coherent policies; Ennahdha describes rising prices and a falling purchasing power. Supporters of direct action say it protects consumers quickly.

tn_echaab.n: Maghzaoui (April 2026) criticised one-off price interventions that do not tackle root causes, and called for coherent policies.

nd.tn_25j: This edition did not open a source documenting the government’s price measures.
nd.tn_nahdha: Ennahdha (January 2026) describes rising prices and weaker purchasing power but proposed no measures in the statement found.

questions.text: Tunisia should speed up its shift to renewable energy so it depends less on gas from Algeria.
questions.ctx: In April 2026 Echaab’s leader asked what gas supply Tunisia can count on by 2030 and about energy relations with Algeria, criticised the lack of official information, and urged the country to anticipate a shift to alternative energy. Supporters of a faster shift cite energy security and costs; others warn that renewables need large investment and that gas will still be needed.

tn_echaab.n: Maghzaoui (April 2026) urged Tunisia to anticipate the move to alternative energy and asked about gas supply and ties with Algeria towards 2030.

nd.tn_25j: This edition found no recent government energy plan in the sources opened.

questions.text: Health, education and public transport should be guaranteed as quality public services rather than opened further to private business.
questions.ctx: The government defends its 2026 budget, partly financed by the Central Bank, as needed to preserve the continuity of public services. Echaab’s leader calls quality public health, education and transport a precondition for democratic progress and opposes treating them as goods for sale. Others argue that private providers can relieve overstretched public services.

tn_echaab.n: Maghzaoui (April 2026) called quality public health, education and transport “a sine qua non of real democratic progress” and opposed treating them as goods for sale.

tn_25j.n: The government defends its 2026 budget strategy as needed to “preserve the continuity of public services” (Ecofin, October 2025).
